questions.stem: A customer success team of twelve people on a Claude Team plan all write renewal emails using the same pricing sheet, objection-handling guide and tone rules. Today each person pastes those files into new chats, and their emails quote different discount terms depending on which version of the files they pasted. The team lead wants every rep working from the same approved material with the LEAST ongoing effort. What should she do?

options.text: Email the latest versions of the three files to the whole team and ask everyone to paste only those copies into each new chat.
Ask each rep to create a personal Project with the three files so their own chats always start from the same material.
Create one Project with the approved files as knowledge and the tone rules as instructions, and share it with the team.
Combine the three files into one long first message that reps copy into every chat before asking for an email.

questions.explanation: The cue is **many people, same material, every time**. A single Project holds the approved files as knowledge and the tone rules as instructions, and every chat started inside it begins with that context. On Team and Enterprise plans the Project can be shared with colleagues, so when the pricing sheet changes the lead updates it in **one place** and everyone picks it up.

whyWrong.A: This still relies on twelve people pasting files by hand into every chat. The next time the pricing sheet changes, old copies sitting in inboxes will cause the same drift.
whyWrong.B: Twelve personal Projects means twelve copies to keep in sync. As soon as one rep forgets to update their copy, the inconsistent discount terms come back.
whyWrong.D: A copy-paste block is the same manual workaround in a different shape. It is easy to skip, easy to edit by accident and has no single owner.

questions.mindset: Shared, repeated context belongs in one shared Project, not in everyone's clipboard.

questions.stem: A grants officer built a Project called 'Foundation Proposals' with instructions to write in a warm, plain-English voice and to keep every summary under 200 words. Later she opens a new chat from the main Claude home screen to draft a proposal summary and gets a 450-word reply in a formal tone. What is the MOST likely explanation and fix?

options.text: Project instructions only apply to chats inside that Project, so she should start the chat from within 'Foundation Proposals'.
The instructions have probably expired after a period of inactivity, so she should paste them back into the Project settings.
The model has drifted from her instructions over time, so she should switch to a more capable model for summaries.
Project instructions are only suggestions, so she should repeat the 200-word limit in capital letters in every message.

questions.explanation: A Project is a **self-contained workspace**. Its instructions and knowledge shape only the chats started inside it. A chat opened from the home screen is outside the Project, so none of her voice or length rules were loaded. The fix is to start the chat inside the Project. If she wanted a rule in *every* conversation, that would belong in her account-wide preferences instead of a single Project.

whyWrong.B: Nothing in how Projects work suggests instructions expire. Re-pasting them into the Project would not affect a chat that was never inside the Project.
whyWrong.C: No model can follow instructions it was never given. The problem is where the chat was started, not how capable the model is.
whyWrong.D: Shouting the rule in every message is a manual workaround. Inside the Project the instructions already apply, so the real fix is starting the chat there.

questions.mindset: Know the scope of each setting: Project instructions stay inside their Project.

questions.stem: During a live video call, an HR coordinator wants to remind herself what the acronym 'OKR' stands for and get a one-sentence explanation she can share with a new hire. The Research toggle is still switched on in her chat from earlier in the day. What is the MOST appropriate way to get the answer?

options.text: Leave Research on so that the one-sentence explanation is backed by several cited sources she can show the new hire.
Create a new Project for HR terminology and ask the question there so the answer is saved for future reference.
Ask Claude to produce the explanation as an artifact so she can edit and share it with the new hire after the call.
Turn Research off and ask in an ordinary chat, since a quick, well-known definition needs no multi-source investigation.

questions.explanation: This is a **quick, stable, well-known fact** needed in seconds. Plain chat is the right tool. Research runs several searches that build on each other and usually takes minutes, and it draws down usage limits faster. That is overkill for one sentence during a live call.

whyWrong.A: Research is built for multi-source investigation and takes minutes. Running it for a one-line definition is slower and uses limits faster with no real benefit.
whyWrong.B: A Project is for recurring work with shared files and instructions. Setting one up for a single definition adds effort without solving anything.
whyWrong.C: Artifacts suit substantial, self-contained output that will be edited or reused. A one-sentence definition does not need that.

questions.mindset: Match the feature to the size of the job: a quick fact is just a chat.

questions.stem: An account director on a Claude Pro plan must prepare for a renewal meeting. She wants one briefing that combines the client's recent public announcements with what has been agreed in her own email threads and meeting notes with that client over the last quarter. Her Google Workspace is connected to Claude. Which approach would MOST effectively produce a sourced briefing with minimal manual gathering?

options.text: Paste the client's latest press release and her five most recent emails into a chat and ask Claude to merge them into a brief.
Use Research with web search and her Google Workspace connectors enabled, then check the cited items before the meeting.
Ask in a regular chat with no tools for a briefing on the client, because Claude already knows about large public companies.
Upload a quarter of exported email threads into a new Project's knowledge and ask Claude to infer the public news from them.

questions.explanation: Research can run several searches that build on each other across the **web** and, when connected, **Gmail, Google Calendar and Google Docs**, and it returns citations. That covers both halves of her need (public news plus internal threads) without hand-collecting material. The citations then make it quick to check the facts that matter before the meeting.

whyWrong.A: Hand-picking a few items is slow and incomplete. Claude can only work with what she happened to paste, so anything she missed is left out.
whyWrong.C: A chat with no tools relies on training data, which may be out of date and has no access to her private email. It also gives her no sources to check.
whyWrong.D: Exporting a quarter of email is heavy manual work, and email threads alone cannot give Claude the client's current public news.

questions.mindset: When the answer spans public sources and your own workspace, use Research with the right connectors, then verify.

questions.stem: A policy analyst at a think tank wants to try Research for a literature scan, but she cannot get it to run on her account. A colleague on the same organization's Claude plan uses Research daily. Which TWO checks should she make FIRST? Choose TWO.

options.text: Confirm she is signed in to her own account on the organization's plan, rather than a personal account outside it.
Rewrite her question in more detail, since Research only runs when a prompt is long enough.
Switch to the most capable model, since Research is limited to the top model tier.
Confirm that web search is turned on, since Research depends on it to run.
Move the literature scan into a Project, since Research works only inside Projects.

questions.explanation: A feature's availability and its settings follow the **account**. The fastest checks are the basics: which account is she actually signed in to (a personal account outside the organization's plan will not carry the organization's features and admin settings, even though her colleague on the plan can use Research), and whether **web search is enabled**, which Research requires to run. Both checks take seconds, and either would explain why the feature works for a colleague but not for her.

whyWrong.B: Research does not depend on prompt length. A clearer question can improve the results, but it cannot make an unavailable feature run.
whyWrong.C: Nothing ties Research to a single model tier. Changing models does not address an account or setting problem.
whyWrong.E: Research is not restricted to Projects. Moving the work into a Project adds setup without addressing why the feature is unavailable.

questions.mindset: When a feature is missing, check which account you are signed in to and its settings before changing how you work.

questions.stem: A training manager has used Claude to build a 12-slide induction deck as an artifact and refined it over several rounds. The client's HR team now says they must present it from their own laptop in a room with no internet connection, using their usual presentation software. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.text: Share a link to the artifact with the HR team so they can open it in their browser on the day of the session.
Copy the slide text from the artifact into a long chat reply so the HR team can rebuild the slides themselves.
Ask Claude to create the deck as a PowerPoint (.pptx) file that the HR team can download and present offline.
Publish the artifact so that it is available at a public link the HR team can reach whenever they need it.

questions.explanation: The constraint is a **specific file format used offline**. Claude can create real Word, Excel, PowerPoint and PDF files using code execution, so the right move is to turn the finished content into a .pptx the client can download and open in their own software. Artifacts are excellent for iterating, but a link does not meet an offline, own-software requirement.

whyWrong.A: An artifact link needs a browser and internet access, which the room does not have. It also isn't a file in their usual presentation software.
whyWrong.B: This pushes the formatting work onto the client and throws away the slides that were already refined.
whyWrong.D: Publishing makes the content reachable online, which does not help in a room with no internet. It may also expose training material more widely than needed.

questions.mindset: If the stakeholder needs a specific file format, deliver that file, not a link.

questions.stem: A sales enablement lead built an AI-powered artifact: a practice tool where reps type a customer objection and the artifact uses Claude to role-play the customer and give feedback. She wants to share it with 40 reps, but worries that their heavy use during a two-week bootcamp will use up her own plan's usage and lock her out of her day-to-day work. What is the MOST accurate guidance?

options.text: She can share it as planned, because each rep's use of the artifact counts against that rep's own plan limits.
She should keep it private and run each rep's practice session herself, so the tool's usage stays under her control.
She should rebuild the tool as a Project, because only Projects keep each user's usage separate from the creator's.
She should ask each rep to copy the artifact's prompt into their own chats, since shared artifacts bill to the creator.

questions.explanation: Per the Claude Help Center, when an artifact calls Claude, the usage **counts against the plan limits of the person using it, not the creator's**. Sharing the practice tool is exactly what AI-powered artifacts are for. Her own limits are not at risk from the reps' practice sessions.

whyWrong.B: Running 40 people's practice herself defeats the purpose of an interactive tool and is based on a wrong assumption about whose usage is counted.
whyWrong.C: Converting to a Project loses the interactive role-play tool, and it rests on the false idea that artifacts bill usage to the creator.
whyWrong.D: This throws away the purpose-built tool for a manual workaround, again based on the mistaken belief that shared artifacts bill the creator.

questions.mindset: Know how a shared feature behaves before inventing a workaround for a problem that doesn't exist.

questions.stem: An independent marketing consultant works with two clients who are direct competitors. Each has its own brand voice, and their strategy documents must never influence the other client's work. She currently does all her work in ordinary chats and has written both clients' tone rules into the account-wide preferences that apply to every conversation. Which TWO changes BEST protect separation and keep each client's voice consistent? Choose TWO.

options.text: Keep a single Project for all consulting work and start every message by naming which client the request is for.
Create a separate Project for each client, holding only that client's documents and work.
Turn on Research for both clients so Claude checks public sources instead of relying on either client's documents.
Switch to the most capable model, which is better at keeping two clients' information apart in shared chats.
Move each client's tone rules out of the account-wide preferences and into that client's Project instructions.

questions.explanation: Each Project is a self-contained workspace with **its own knowledge, instructions and chat history**, separate from other Projects and from ordinary chats. One Project per client keeps their documents apart. Account-wide preferences apply to **every** conversation, so both clients' tone rules currently compete in every chat, including inside any Project she creates. Moving each set into the matching Project's instructions gives each client a consistent voice with no cross-influence.

whyWrong.A: One shared Project puts both competitors' documents in the same knowledge base and relies on her remembering a label every time. That is exactly the leakage she wants to avoid.
whyWrong.C: Research is for multi-source investigation. It does nothing to separate client material or apply the right voice.
whyWrong.D: A bigger model is not a separation control. The fix is structural: keep each client's material in its own workspace.

questions.mindset: Separate sensitive contexts structurally, and put rules at the narrowest scope where they apply.

questions.stem: A compliance analyst on a Claude Team plan wants to ask everyday questions about her company's 180 internal policy documents. A colleague warns her that 'Claude can't hold that much at once', and suggests several workarounds. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.text: Split the policies into six Projects of 30 documents each and decide which Project to ask before every question.
Ask Claude to write a one-paragraph summary of each policy and upload only the summaries so everything fits.
Keep the policies out of Claude and paste the relevant section into a new chat each time she has a question.
Upload the policies to one Project's knowledge and let Claude retrieve relevant sections, checking the source passages for key answers.

questions.explanation: On paid plans, when Project knowledge is too large to fit in context at once, Claude **automatically switches to retrieval (RAG)**, searching the knowledge for the sections relevant to each question. That greatly expands how much a Project can hold while keeping quality. One Project with all the policies is simplest. Because compliance answers matter, she should still check the passages behind important answers.

whyWrong.A: Manually splitting the library means she must guess the right Project for each question, and cross-policy questions break. Built-in retrieval already handles the size.
whyWrong.B: One-paragraph summaries lose the exact wording that compliance questions depend on, so answers would be less reliable.
whyWrong.C: Hand-pasting sections is slow and only works if she already knows where the answer is. That defeats the point of asking Claude.

questions.mindset: Don't build manual workarounds for limits the product already handles; just keep verifying high-stakes answers.

questions.stem: A program director produces a quarterly impact report for her board. Each quarter she reuses the same report template, last year's reports and the board's style preferences, and the draft goes through several rounds of edits with her CEO before it is sent. Which TWO features BEST support this workflow? Choose TWO.

options.text: Research mode, so that Claude collects the program's internal figures from public sources and cites each one.
A single ongoing chat that she reuses every quarter so the history of past reports is always visible to Claude.
A Project holding the template and past reports as knowledge, with the board's style rules written as instructions.
An artifact for the report draft, so it sits beside the chat and can be revised round by round and then shared.
The most capable model for every step, because board reports are important enough to need the strongest model.

questions.explanation: Two cues point to two features. **Recurring, same materials, same rules** points to a Project with knowledge and instructions. **A substantial document edited over several rounds and then shared** points to an artifact, which opens beside the chat for iterative editing and sharing. Together they cover setup and output with no manual workaround.

whyWrong.A: Her internal program figures are not on the public web. Research is for multi-source investigation, not for finding numbers only her organization holds.
whyWrong.B: One endless chat grows long, drifts and eventually hits length limits. A Project gives each quarter a fresh chat with the same stored context.
whyWrong.E: Model choice is a separate question from feature choice, and 'strongest for everything' ignores cost and speed. It does not organize the materials or the drafts.

questions.mindset: Map each cue to its feature: repeated context to a Project, an iterated deliverable to an artifact.

questions.stem: A communications officer has a one-page media policy in an artifact that her manager has already approved, except for one paragraph about social media that legal wants softened. She is worried that asking Claude to 'revise the policy' will also change wording that was already signed off. What is the MOST reliable way to make the change?

options.text: Ask Claude to regenerate the whole policy with a softer tone, then compare the new and old versions line by line.
Highlight just the social media paragraph in the artifact and ask Claude to revise only that selection.
Copy the full policy into a new chat and tell Claude to rewrite it while being careful with the other paragraphs.
Switch to a more capable model, which is less likely to change approved paragraphs when revising a document.

questions.explanation: Artifacts support **targeted edits**: you can highlight specific text and ask Claude to change only that part. Scoping the change to the one paragraph legal flagged is the most reliable way to leave the approved wording untouched. It is a built-in control rather than relying on Claude to 'be careful'.

whyWrong.A: Regenerating everything invites changes across the whole document and then makes her hunt for them. That adds review work and risk.
whyWrong.C: Asking Claude to 'be careful' is a soft instruction that does not limit what can change, and moving to a new chat leaves the approved artifact behind.
whyWrong.D: Model strength does not limit the scope of an edit. The precise tool here is selecting the exact text to revise.

questions.mindset: When only part of a deliverable should change, scope the edit to that part.

questions.stem: A school administrator finds a published artifact made by a colleague at another campus: an interactive timetable planner. She wants a version adapted to her campus's bell schedule, but the colleague's staff rely on the original every day. What is the MOST appropriate approach?

options.text: Ask the colleague for edit access and change the original planner to her own campus's bell schedule.
Take screenshots of the planner and ask Claude in a new chat to describe what each screen does.
Ask the colleague to add a toggle for her campus to the original, so both campuses share one planner.
Copy the published artifact as a starting point and describe her campus's changes, creating her own version.

questions.explanation: Published artifacts can be **copied as a starting point**. The copy is an independent version, so she can adapt it to her bell schedule without affecting the original the other campus depends on. It is the lowest-effort, lowest-risk path.

whyWrong.A: Editing the original would break the planner the other campus uses every day.
whyWrong.B: Screenshots and descriptions throw away the working tool and force her to rebuild from scratch.
whyWrong.C: This puts her request on someone else's workload and risks changing a tool others depend on, when she can make her own copy.

questions.mindset: Reuse safely: build your version from a copy and leave others' working tools alone.

questions.stem: An office manager keeps the company's employee handbook and benefits guide in a Claude Project used by the people team. An employee asks how many days of bereavement leave the company offers. The office manager is about to turn on Research to make sure the answer is 'properly sourced'. What should she do instead?

options.text: Ask the question in a chat inside the Project and confirm the answer against the handbook section it is based on.
Use Research with web search so Claude can compare the company's policy with common practice at other companies.
Ask in a fresh chat outside the Project so that the answer is not influenced by older documents in the knowledge base.
Ask Claude to draft the reply as an artifact so the employee can see the full policy text alongside the answer.

questions.explanation: The answer lives in **the company's own handbook**, which is already in the Project's knowledge. Asking inside the Project grounds the reply in that document, and checking the handbook section behind it takes seconds. Research searches the web and connected sources for a multi-angle investigation. It may pull in general practice from elsewhere and draws down usage limits faster, which is the wrong tool for 'what does our policy say?'.

whyWrong.B: Other companies' practices do not answer what this company offers, and outside sources could muddy a simple policy fact.
whyWrong.C: Leaving the Project removes the handbook from the conversation, so Claude would be guessing instead of reading the policy.
whyWrong.D: An artifact changes how the reply looks, not where the answer comes from. A short policy answer does not need one.

questions.mindset: For 'what do our documents say', ask where the documents are, not on the open web.

questions.stem: A bid manager on a Claude Team plan has a Project containing confidential pricing models and draft proposal text for a major tender. Four bid team members need to draft with it, and two senior reviewers need to read the material and ask Claude questions, but must not change the instructions or files. Which TWO sharing choices BEST fit this situation? Choose TWO.

options.text: Make the Project visible to the whole organization so anyone who might help with the bid can find it quickly.
Give the four bid team members 'Can edit' access so they can update knowledge and instructions as the bid evolves.
Give everyone, reviewers included, 'Can edit' access so nobody is blocked if they spot something they want to change.
Export the knowledge files and email them to the reviewers so they can read the material without Project access.
Invite only the named people and give the two senior reviewers 'Can view' access to the Project.

questions.explanation: Project sharing on Team and Enterprise plans has two levels. **Can edit** lets members change instructions and knowledge. **Can view** lets members see the content and chat in the Project without editing it. Inviting only the named people keeps confidential pricing to the bid team. Giving reviewers view access meets their need to read and ask questions while protecting the files and instructions.

whyWrong.A: Organization-wide visibility exposes confidential pricing to people with no need to see it. That is a governance failure, even if it is convenient.
whyWrong.C: Edit access for reviewers directly contradicts the requirement that they must not change instructions or files.
whyWrong.D: Emailing confidential files creates uncontrolled copies outside Claude, and reviewers lose the ability to question the material in the Project.

questions.mindset: Share with the fewest people at the lowest permission that still lets them do their job.

questions.stem: A regional sales manager wants her team to stop doing discount calculations by hand. She describes the rules to Claude (volume tiers, a cap for new customers and a manager-approval flag above a threshold) and wants something reps can open, enter a deal size into and see the allowed discount. Which output is MOST appropriate?

options.text: A long chat reply listing every rule in a table that reps can scroll back to whenever they need to work out a discount.
An interactive artifact that applies the rules, which she can test with real deal examples before sharing with the team.
A new Project containing the discount rules as instructions, so reps can ask Claude to calculate each discount in chat.
A Research report on discount practices across her industry, so reps understand how competitors price similar deals.

questions.explanation: She needs a **small, reusable tool**: enter a number, get an answer. Artifacts can be interactive tools that open beside the chat, are refined over iterations and can be shared. Testing it on real deals before rollout checks that the rules were captured correctly.

whyWrong.A: A table still leaves reps doing the arithmetic by hand, which is the very problem she wants to remove.
whyWrong.C: A Project works, but each rep would need to ask Claude for every deal, and the answer could vary with wording. A tool that applies the rules is faster and more consistent.
whyWrong.D: Industry research does not calculate her company's allowed discount. It answers a different question.

questions.mindset: When people need to reuse a small tool, build the tool, then test it before sharing.
